statement: A box holds 4 red, 5 blue and 6 green balls, mixed up. How many must be taken out without looking to be sure of having 3 of the same colour?

choices.misconception: I answered with the luckiest case, where the first three balls happen to match.
I found the worst case of two of each colour and forgot to take one more.
I multiplied the three colours by the three balls I need, rather than thinking about the worst case.
I worked from the number of balls of each colour rather than from the number of colours.

hints: What is the unluckiest possible draw?
Ask how many balls you could take while still not holding three of any one colour. One more than that number forces a third of some colour, because there is nowhere new for it to go.
The worst case is two of each colour, which is 6 balls and still no set of three. The seventh ball must make a third of some colour.

solutions.reliable: Think about the worst case, not the lucky one. You could draw two red, two blue and two green - six balls with no colour appearing three times. But a seventh ball has to be red, blue or green, and whichever it is, that colour now has three. So 7 balls guarantee it and 6 do not. The transferable idea: fill every box to one short of the target, then add one.
solutions.elegant: With 3 colours acting as boxes, 7 balls cannot be spread with at most 2 per box, since 3 x 2 = 6.

whyOnTest: To be sure means the worst case, and the answer is always one more than the largest arrangement that still fails.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
